pll1d42c3-d1e3501.summary: Concludes with Hugh of St Victor that omnipotence appears in two ways: God does all he wills and suffers nothing. Nothing can corrupt or impede him; he can do all except what would harm his dignity, which is not power but impotence. So none should call God impotent in anything; he can do all that it is power to be able to do.
claims: God does all he wills and suffers nothing.
Inability to do what would harm his dignity is not impotence.

pll1d42c3-d1e3513.summary: Notes that some authorities say God is truly omnipotent because he can do whatever he wills.

pll1d42c3-d1e3516.summary: Cites the Enchiridion: God is called omnipotent for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills, and no creature's will impedes the effect of the omnipotent will.
claims: God is omnipotent because he can do whatever he wills.
No creature can impede God's will.

pll1d42c3-d1e3537.summary: Cites De spiritu et littera: God cannot do unjust things, being supreme justice and goodness; he is omnipotent not because he can do all things but because he can do whatever he wills, and nothing can resist or impede his will.
claims: God cannot do injustice.
Nothing can resist God's will.

pll1d42c3-d1e3554.summary: Cites Chrysostom on the Creed: God is called omnipotent because his power cannot meet impotence; he did all he willed (Ps 113:11); no one resists his will (Rom 9:19).
claims: God's power meets no impotence.

pll1d42c3-d1e3614.summary: Notes that these authorities seem to show that God is called omnipotent only because he can do all he wills, not because he can do all things.

pll1d42c3-d1e3618.summary: Answers that Augustine took 'all things' so broadly as to include evils, which God neither wills nor can do, without denying that he can do all that befits him. 'Omnipotent for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills' does not deny he can do what he does not will, but answers those who said God wills much he cannot do.
claims: Augustine's 'all things' included evils.
He opposed those who held God wills what he cannot do.

pll1d42c3-d1e3642.summary: Warns against misreading 'he can do whatever he wills to be done.' If it meant 'whatever he wills himself to be able to do,' Peter or any saint would be omnipotent, since they can do what they will to do; but they cannot do all they will to be done, as they will the salvation of the saved but cannot save them. God can do whatever he wills to be done, by himself (as heaven and earth) or through creatures (as houses through humans); humans or angels are not powerful by or from themselves.
claims: Saints can do what they will to do but not all they will to be done.
God can do all he wills to be done, directly or through creatures.
Creatures are not powerful by themselves.

pll1d42c3-d1e3645.summary: Objection: only the Father can act from himself, being from himself; the Son is from the Father and the Spirit from both.

pll1d42c3-d1e3648.summary: Answers that though the Son cannot act from himself, he can act through himself, and so the Spirit.
claims: Son and Spirit act through themselves, not from themselves.

pll1d42c3-d1e3651.summary: Cites Hilary: the unity of nature is such that the Son acts through himself without acting from himself. He acts through himself by having the same natural power as the Father, received from the Father. Humans and angels have gratuitous power.
claims: The Son has the same natural power as the Father, received from him.
Creatures have gratuitous power.

pll1d42c3-d1e3671.summary: Concludes that the Trinity is truly and properly omnipotent because by itself, by natural power, it can do whatever it wills to be done and whatever it wills itself to be able. It wills nothing to be done that it cannot do itself or through creatures; it wills to be able to do all it wills done, but does not will done all it wills to be able, or it would be done, since nothing resists its will.
claims: God can do whatever he wills by natural power.
God wills to be able to do more than he wills to be done.
Nothing resists God's will.

pl-l1d42c3.summary: Concludes, following Hugh of St Victor, that omnipotence has two aspects: God does all he wills and suffers nothing; he can do all except what would harm his dignity, which is no lack, since such 'power' would be impotence. Some authorities (Augustine's Enchiridion and De spiritu et littera, Chrysostom) say God is omnipotent only because he can do whatever he wills, not because he can do all things. Lombard reads them as excluding evils, which God neither wills nor can do, and as answering those who said God wills much he cannot do. 'He can do whatever he wills to be done' must not be read as 'whatever he wills himself to be able to do,' which would make Peter omnipotent: saints can do what they will to do but not all they will to be done. God can do whatever he wills by himself, directly or through creatures. The Son and Spirit act not from themselves but through themselves, with the same natural power received from the Father (Hilary), while humans and angels have gratuitous power. So the Trinity is properly omnipotent: it can, by natural power, do whatever it wills to be done and whatever it wills itself to be able.
claims: Omnipotence means God does all he wills and suffers nothing.
God can do all things except what would harm his dignity, which is not a lack of power.
'Omnipotent because he can do whatever he wills' excludes evil and answers those who limited God's power.
Saints can do what they will to do but not all they will to be done; God can.
The Son and Spirit act through themselves, not from themselves, by natural power from the Father.
Creatures have gratuitous, not natural, power.
The Trinity is omnipotent by natural power to do whatever it wills.
